analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurance plans to cover medically necessary reconstructive surgery.
analysis.headline: The bill to require insurance coverage for reconstructive surgery never got a committee vote; it sat in two House committees until Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal health insurance rules so that any employer health plan or individual insurance policy covering surgery must also cover reconstructive surgery — operations to repair damage from birth defects, injuries, infections, tumors, or disease, either to restore function or to restore a normal appearance. It explicitly does not require coverage for cosmetic surgery done simply to improve looks on a normal body. If it had become law, it would have applied to plan years starting on or after January 1, 2008, with a phase-in for plans run under existing union contracts.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients whose bodies are altered by congenital defects, accidents, burns, infections, cancer, or disease — people who today can face insurance denials because the surgery to restore function or normal appearance is labeled cosmetic. Requiring coverage would shift those medical costs onto group health plans and individual-market insurers, and ultimately into premiums spread across enrollees.

how_it_helps.text: Amends the Public Health Service Act and ERISA so any group health plan that covers surgery must also cover reconstructive surgery, including medically necessary pre- and post-operative care ordered by the treating physician [S2] [S3].

Defines reconstructive surgery as medically necessary operations to correct abnormal body structures from congenital defects, developmental abnormalities, trauma, infection, tumors, or disease, to improve function or give a normal appearance [S2] [S3].
Applies the same coverage requirement to health insurance sold in the individual market, so people buying their own coverage are protected too [S2] [S3].
Explicitly excludes cosmetic surgery on normal body structures, limiting the mandate to medical repair rather than appearance enhancement [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers sponsoring health plans, insurers selling group and individual coverage, and enrollees through somewhat higher premiums; also plans run under pre-existing union contracts, which get a delayed effective date.

drawbacks.text: The mandate raises health costs for employers and insurers, which typically pass through to premiums paid by workers and individual policyholders, including people who never need such surgery [S3].

The line between reconstructive and cosmetic surgery — giving the patient a normal appearance — is judged by the operating physician, which gives insurers limited ability to police claims and could invite boundary disputes and cost growth [S3].

The bill takes no position on how coverage interacts with existing state mandates or with the cost of plans overall, and it contains no provisions addressing premiums or cost-sharing for consumers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients facing disfigurement or loss of function, the benefit is concrete and large; the cost is a modest, spread-out premium increase. The main design weakness is the physician-judged boundary between reconstructive and cosmetic work, which leaves room for disputes. On balance a fairly narrow, targeted mandate rather than a sweeping expansion.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to two House committees and their health subcommittees, and neither ever reported it out, so it never reached the House floor before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Mike Ross (D-AR) introduced the bill on June 21, 2007 [S1] [S5].
The same day it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Education and Labor Committee [S5].
It was then referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and, in September 2007, to the Education and Labor Subcommittee on Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
No further action was taken, and the bill died at the end of the 110th Congress without a committee vote or floor action [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and health insurers avoided a new federal coverage mandate, and patients needing reconstructive surgery got no federal guarantee; the status quo on coverage denials stood.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers avoiding a mandate

for.name: Rep. Mike Ross
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 19 cosponsors

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral with jurisdiction over public health insurance rules
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to its Health Subcommittee, and never acted on it

against.name: House Education and Labor Committee
against.role: Second committee of referral with jurisdiction over ERISA-covered plans
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to its Health, Employment, Labor, and Pensions Subcommittee, and never acted on it

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was 16 Democrats and 3 Republicans plus a Democratic sponsor, but the bill's death in committee left no votes to measure partisan support.

industries.note: The bill would force insurers to cover reconstructive surgery they can currently deny, adding to their claims costs. Patients needing these operations benefit directly from the requirement.
ERISA plans would face the same coverage mandate, raising benefits costs for employers; the delay for plans under existing union contracts softens the immediate hit.
A coverage mandate would expand the pool of reimbursable procedures for surgeons performing medically necessary reconstruction.
